power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Self-other evaluations play a crucial role in understanding psychiatric disorders and improving collaboration between service users and providers.
However, experimental paradigms of such relational processes tend to have low reliability and ecological validity.
Quantitative analyses can validate the task's measurement properties while qualitative analyses can empower service users to provide novel insights about task development and interpretation.
In this study, we use both quantitative and qualitative analyses to develop the "Helping Task" based on the iterated prisoner's dilemma.
In this task, help-seeking participants knowingly engaged in an asymmetric relationship with a computerized helpprovider, in which both parties invested effort (points).

Initial qualitative feedback from 17 individuals (15 'neurotypical', 2 having lived experience of relational difficulties) was used to refine key task properties (like task instructions, interface labels, and general navigation).

Subsequent thematic analyses revealed that these participants interpreted helping exchanges through expectations about reciprocity, moral obligations, and underlying mental intentions, mirroring descriptions of real helping relationships.

Moreover, quantitative analyses of 30 online participants validated the task's sensitivity to helper behaviour and the within-session reliability of mean trust, decision satisfaction, and intended effort.

Finally, computational analyses revealed probabilistic states in which trust, decision satisfaction, and effort were jointly lower or higher, indicating that self-other evaluations were linked to willingness to invest in the relationship.
These findings support the reliability and validity of the Helping Task and pave the way for computational studies of self-other evaluations in helping relationships.
Help-seeking involves translating a privately perceived need into something interpersonal, reaching out to another person for support (Rickwood et al., 2005).

text.text: Help-seeking is a highstakes form of social interaction.
In many cases, help-seeking presents an asymmetric dynamic; the help-seeker, e.g. an ill patient, enters a more vulnerable position and bears more risk.
Hence many who need help do not engage with it, or do so unsuccessfully.
This may be due to lack of information, but also due to embarrassment or mistrust (Elshaikh et al., 2023; Gulliver et al., 2010; Huff et al., 2024).

text.text: Computational psychiatry is a promising discipline which has recently sought to elucidate trust.
It combines neuroscience and economics, which together reveal brain processes behind behaviour and decision-making (Rilling and Sanfey, 2011).

text.text: It clarifies how people learn, pursue reward, and trade off exploration against exploitation (Daw et al., 2006).

text.text: These processes become more complex in social settings, where a person controls only part of the outcome.
Repeated economic games, such as the multi-round Investor-Trustee task (MRITT), show how cooperation is built and how it breaks down or is repaired (Guennouni et al., 2026; King-Casas et al., 2005).

Inference is also applied to the self, so that a person infers their own worth in much the same way as they infer the trustworthiness of others (Moutoussis, Fearon, et al., 2014; Will et al., 2017).

text.text: Creating rigorous tasks is only half the work; the settings used to elicit mental states matter just as much for ecological validity and real-world relevance.
Neuroeconomic tasks have been critiqued to lack ecological validity and in some cases also reliability (Colman, 2003; Schilbach et al., 2013; Zavlis et al., 2025).

text.text: Some rely on deception (the deceive-thendebrief approach), which soon becomes known and hence fair game to 'game'.
At present, neurocomputational studies of trust, especially those about being helped, remain limited in ecological validity and in relevance to the people who use services.
Little work has integrated qualitative and quantitative data of mentalizing and trust in interpersonal dynamics.

Pioneering work from our team (Lau et al., 2024) asked whether and why people trusted professionals with their social evaluation learning task (SELT), but the task was neither interactive nor designed to account for the greater vulnerability of help-seekers.

text.text: To address these issues and examine self-and other-evaluations during help-seeking interactions, we developed a new task based on the iterated prisoner's dilemma, but involving a realistic framing and assessments of subjective experience.
Rigorous understanding of trust as emotion and decision-making is very challenging, as it involves setting, hot (emotion-rich) cognition and decision-making under risk.
Indeed, individual differences shape expectations, the environment, and even what 'trusting a helper' means.
One's definition of trust can be a discursive representation of one's track record of betrayal (Driver, 2015; Trotsuk, 2016).

text.text: To select the aspects of this complex landscape which would make the 'Helping Task' most relevant and valid, in recent work we consulted with Experts by Experience of help-seeking for Functional Neurological Disorder (FND).
They largely corroborated the above.
They advised us to ask participants to rate their trust in their helper, and their satisfaction with themselves, as well as their decisions, within the 'Helping Task'.
We proceeded to collect and model ratings of trust and decision satisfaction, alongside qualitative structured recall narratives.

We first examined whether detailed qualitative study of our novel 'Helping Task' would not only make it meaningful and user-friendly to potential participants, but would help uncover modes of experience and thinking of help-seekers that have not as yet informed rigorous laboratory studies of trust.
Second, we examined whether attending to the epistemic standpoint of individuals with lived experience of relationship difficulties (LE) would substantially enrich this understanding.
Third, we assessed whether the key outputs of the task, that is, decisions to invest effort, decision satisfaction and trust, were sensitive to helper behaviour and reliable within a session.
Finally, we explored whether patterns in help-seekers' evaluations and behaviour could be described using hidden Markov models.

To address these aims, we conducted: 1. thematic analyses of interviews with selfreported 'neurotypical' participants to elucidate key elements of trust, such as the object (who's being trusted), domain (what they're being trusted for), and sources of trust (i.e., traditions, rational reasons, etc.

text.text: We conducted two studies with the Helping Task.
In Study 1, we used qualitative methods to elucidate key experiential perspectives in help-seeking and develop the task (n = 17).

We first administered the task to a convenience sample, which we call '(neuro)typical participants' (TP, n = 15), on the basis that they did not report serious relationship difficulties and reported being physically and mentally healthy.
They played the task in full on their computers or laptops and then discussed it over Zoom.
The first five provided task feedback; the remaining 10 completed interviews.
Nine interview recordings were available for thematic analysis because one recording was lost.

After implementing the changes based on the task feedback of the TP group, we sought feedback from two individuals with lived experience (LE) of relationship difficulties, accompanied by full playthroughs of the task.
In Study 2, we recruited a total of 30 participants from the Prolific Academic platform (prolific.com).
The participants gave written informed consent and were paid at an hourly rate approved by the Ethics Committee (110% of the minimum wage at the time of study).
All participants were adults aged 18-65 who could speak, read and write English fluently; self-reported demographics are given in Table 1.

text.text: Before beginning the experiment, participants were informed that they would be paired with a computerized helper agent, and asked to interact with it as if it were a real person, while role-playing as the help-seeker.

They first went through a set of instructions explaining the task, and were given time to explore the asymmetrical reward consequences of the various combinations of effort invested between the helper and themselves.
The Helping Task is described in Figure 1 and was adapted from a probabilistic iterated prisoner's dilemma used in a prior study (Moutoussis et al., 2025).

We were interested in whether participants could put themselves 'in the shoes' of the real situation, or whether they treated it as an impersonal game; whether they found the task easy to understand, immersive (i.e., in the sense that they were genuinely compelled to think about their helper as caring, helpful, etc.), engaging (i.e., whether they could fully attend to the needs of the situation), and ecologically valid (both the interpersonal dynamics and helper behaviours).
We were also interested in specific elements of the task design and initial instructions and practice rounds, e.g., whether bar graphs were the best way to illustrate the noisy effort distributions.
Participants were given space to discuss any additional concerns.
We asked participants to note important feelings and moments with the helper.
After each block of trials, they recalled these notes and evaluated the helper.

The interviews were semi-structured, guided flexibly by questions (e.g., "What do you think of the helper?"), and designed to understand the participant's subjective experience, for example, how participants made sense of events like being let down or helped.
Interviews were intended to elicit participants' own thoughts and feelings without suggesting interpretations.
Interviews were conducted over Zoom, and participants consented to recording for transcription.
We implemented the thematic analysis framework (an inductive, semantic, and realist approach) described by Braun and Clarke (2006; Table 2).

text.text: Participant interviews were first transcribed and reviewed repeatedly to develop an in-depth understanding of the data.
The initial round of coding was completed, annotating semantic features regarding the participant's experience.
After coding, the entire list was compiled to identify patterns and similarities and review the coded extracts in each group, considering whether they formed a coherent pattern.
Where codes could be separated into distinct themes, or candidate themes were closely related, they were reassessed as separate themes or subthemes of a broader pattern.
This refining process drew on Patton's (1990) dual criteria for judging categories (internal homogeneity and external heterogeneity).

text.text: They explained their own and the helpers' behaviour not only with respect to trial-to-trial outcomes but also through beliefs about intentions, mutual obligations, and the likely future of the relationship.
The theme 'relational dynamics' was characterized by expectations held for helpseekers and helpers, and their potential influence over each other.
Participants often described normative beliefs about what a helper should do and what they themselves were entitled or obliged to do when asking for help.

These expectations were sometimes learned within the task (i.e., "I realized that I probably have to play nice") or drawn from more general beliefs about deservingness and reciprocity in help-seeking (i.e., "I'm the one asking for help [...]
I don't feel entitled to anyone's help").
In some cases, these expectations were used as a reference to explain why they felt the helper was a good or bad person.
Participants also considered how their own actions might shape the helper's subsequent behaviour, for example by coaxing the helper.
Participants described their decision making with several strategic orientations.
We identified five main types that differed in tolerance to loss and degree of self-and otherregard: coaxing, investing conservatively, barely reciprocating, not cooperating, and freeriding.
Participants used three characteristics to evaluate the helper's 'helpfulness' or trustworthiness: cooperation, consistency, and conscientiousness.

These accounts distinguished observed behaviour from inferred motivation: participants could value a helper's good intentions even when outcomes were less than optimal, while repeated high investment was not always interpreted as genuine cooperation.
Participants described how these evaluations related to their expectations of the helper and their emotions about the exchanges, their helpers, or themselves.
Finally, emotional responses often reflected a violation of helper expectations.
For example, disappointment followed unmet expectations of effort; betrayal involved the perceived violation of an assumed cooperative agreement.
Frustration arose when participants felt unable to act according to their preferred level of investment or unable to change an unresponsive partner.
Regret and pride were self-evaluative, often concerning whether one had acted 'appropriately' toward a helper.
Together, these accounts suggest that participants evaluated outcomes in relation to expectations about themselves and their partners' intentions and actions.

text.text: Both LE participants drew inferences about the helper from small changes in contributions.
They described being reminded of previous relationship problems, making character or moral evaluations, or turning inwards on themselves and their self-worth.

One participant maintained trust in a generally cooperative helper after a single, modest reduction in contribution, while becoming dissatisfied with her own decision to trust: "I felt like I'm a bit stupid because I just trust other people too easily".
She described feeling betrayed, while also considering whether the helper "had a bad day" and maintaining that they were still reliable.
She also distinguished between the two caring helpers: one appeared to be insufficiently caring because they did not seem engaged or invested in her.
Conversely, the other helper was deemed more caring but less helpful.
This distinction separated evaluations of competence or reliability from evaluations of care and moral intention.

A helper could be judged imperfectly helpful while still seeming engaged and therefore trustworthy; alternatively, a helper could be producing positive outcomes but be experienced as emotionally disengaged or uncaring.
The second participant, similarly, characterized even a caring helper as insufficiently attentive to her needs.
She emphasized reciprocity as the cornerstone of cooperation.

In a block with an uncaring helper that she initially described as effective and cooperative, she interpreted the growing inequality in contributions through the experience of a previous friendship and reduced her investment when reciprocity appeared unlikely.
Reflecting on this helper interaction, she also attributed some blame to herself: "Maybe it's also like my issue… I also think I have some trust issues".
Together, these interviews add examples of relational inferences that could be understood in terms of mentalizing.
Participants drew conclusions about helper reliability, character, reciprocity, and their own self-worth, sometimes after small fluctuations in helper behaviour.
The TP and LE interviews revealed several expectations shared across participants from both groups.
Help-seekers emphasised reciprocity, moral obligations, and the importance of feeling that the helper cared.
Participants often described helping in moral rather than purely descriptive terms, discussing what helpers and help-seekers should do and evaluating themselves and others as good or bad people.

Self-directed emotions, including guilt and shame in the LE interviews, arose when participants felt they had violated their own standards, such as by failing to reciprocate, trusting too quickly, or contributing unwillingly to relationships.

Acknowledging the limited statistical power of this study, we explored associations between task responses and personality and mentalizing scores.

We found zero-order associations between antagonism and smaller reductions in decision satisfaction (r=-0.44, p=0.023), and between disinhibition and smaller reductions in decision satisfaction (r=-0.39, p=0.045), following the change from a caring to an uncaring helper.
Both associations were similar using rank correlations and remained negative when individual participants were omitted.

While these associations did not survive correction for multiple comparisons (q=0.612 and 0.808, respectively), these exploratory patterns raise the possibility that personality traits relate to how help-seekers evaluate their own decisions after being let down.

In this study, we validated the Helping Task, an experimental procedure for assessing how help-seekers engage in constructive risk-taking from a vulnerable position as well as how they appraise a simulated 'helper' and themselves.
Importantly, our participants were not deceived about their helpers being computerized avatars but were asked to role-play as help-seekers.
We first sought to improve ecological validity, endorsed by individuals with lived experience with relational difficulties.

Interviewing our lived experience and 'neurotypical' participants suggested that they were immersed in the situation, engaging as if it were real and comparable to real social interactions from their experience.
Moreover, they described engaging in mentalizing processes, described the helper's mental states and/or thinking in more complex ways than they are programmed to behave.
In more detail, our qualitative analyses showed that help-seekers held various expectations of moral, role-based, and relational responsibilities, which shaped their emotions and decision-making.

These findings were paired with exploratory quantitative analyses which identified patterns of trust, self-satisfaction, and engagement suggesting that participants did not "gamify" but rather perceived the task as if it were a real social interaction.
In a recent systematic review from our team, no theory-driven empirical study of interpersonal dynamics in psychopathology reported task reliability (Zavlis et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In a recent systematic review from our team, no theory-driven empirical study of interpersonal dynamics in psychopathology reported task reliability <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Zavlis et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, as Hedge and colleagues (2018) implied, many popular task paradigms produce robust and easily replicable experimental effects simply due to low between-subject variance.
This can make large differences in the qualitative interpretations that can be made from such findings, which may seriously undermine many published conclusions.

Here, we've addressed these problems by demonstrating the consistency within the average scores of our task, while also the differentiation in individual differences from across trust, satisfaction, and effort on a trial-to-trial basis.
Higher effort was strongly associated higher trust and satisfaction scores within session blocks (though more so for the latter).
Indeed, participants were sensitive to helper behaviour, engaging more and reporting higher across both scores with caring helpers than uncaring helpers.
However, as our qualitative findings also suggest, these measures should be separate.

For example, separate measures of trust and satisfaction have demonstrated participants' ability to evaluate their own decision separate from the helper, sometimes to the detriment of their own self-esteem.
Together, these pieces of evidence support the within-session measurement and responsiveness of our task (but leave unvalidated other aspects of the task; see limitations for details).
In our Helping task, participants were not deceived about being paired with artificial helpers and still reported their interactions to be realistic (though see also our limitations).

As we've shown, participants often described their interactions in relational terms, and as if interacting with a conscious being, i.e., reciprocity, helper/help-seeker responsibilities, betrayal, helpers 'having a bad day', countless attempts to make sense of underlying intentions, and quite interestingly, using moral evaluations (e.g., "I wouldn't think he's a bad person or something because, based on the previous evidence, I think he's quite reliable").

Our results are consistent with a wealth of findings indicating that humans apply social expectations (i.e., politeness and reciprocity) to machines without requiring a belief that the computer possesses a mind (Nass & Moon, 2000); that moral judgements depend on perceived intentions, obligations, and the capacity to prevent an outcome (Malle et al., 2014); and the dimensions of experience (relating to moral concern) vs agency (relating moral responsibility) predicate different moral judgments to human and nonhuman characters (Gray, Gray, & Wegner, 2007).

text.text: Indeed, our results suggest that participants anthropomorphize their artificial helpers with a moral typecasting that Gray and Wagner (2009) suggest stems from the nature of dyadic morality.

text.text: Moreover, they behave and reflect on their helper as if it has intentions-and try to infer what they are-as a basis for their moral judgements (i.e., whether the helping agent is caring or not).

Together, these findings align with the wide literature, in support of the ecological validity of our task, and suggest that deception is not necessary to elicit behaviors as one would with other people.
Finally, our hidden Markov analyses were able to recover interpretable latent states from help-seekers' self-and other-evaluations and decisions.
Across samples, the states formed a graded scale ordered by trust, effort and satisfaction together, with trust separating them most clearly.
Participants moved along this scale in response to their helper, rather than playing the task as an impersonal points game.

Again, specific helpertypes reliably shaped the trajectory of our recovered mental states; participants moved towards high-trust states with caring helpers and towards low-trust states with uncaring helpers, whereas participants with random helpers spread across states without any consistent direction.

Trust also built gradually, but broke down sharply, as expected, according to definitions of trust as a (gradually developing) state of accepted vulnerability based on the positive expectations of another's intentions (Rousseau et al., 1998).

text.text: This account is in line with participant accounts of "betrayal" and may explain why feeling betrayed was so devastating to trust, compared to other cases of low effort contributions from a helper.

In recent work, participant-level HMMs were used to identify return behaviors in a repeated trust game. Guennouni and colleagues (2026) showed that a cognitive intervention reduced the tendency to remain in low-return starts following trust withdrawal.

text.text: Adapted from a prisoner's dilemma task, the Helping task shares with the repeated trust game, an emphasis on the persistence, breakdown, and recovery of trust.
However, the application of a cognitive intervention for trust in help-seeking may be more challenging for the same reasons that it is prescribed in the first place.

Nonetheless, as we have seen, interpersonal interactions in help-seeking significantly shape the trajectory of help itself, so some improvement or organization of interpersonal skills is likely to be helpful.

This was the documented case of Hale and Aarts (2023) who found that patients that improved in depression scores from psychotherapy were characterized by longer time spent in states of focused listening.

text.text: Thus, while response profiles (i.e. average effort investment) may be informative, further psychological mechanisms, specifically of interpersonal processes, such as mentalization, require further testing.
Despite these strengths of our study, several limitations must be acknowledged.

Here, we highlight three, particularly the constraints of a small sample size, the need to extend this study with a theory-driven approach, and the ecological differences of interacting with artificial agents compared to real people.
Firstly, this was a pilot study, using a convenience-sampled majority in the case of our qualitative study, and only a pair of lived experience individuals.
The contributions from these groups may be informative for task validity and development, but further support is needed.

In a previous quantitative study from our team (Moutoussis et al., 2025), a power analysis suggested a sample size of 63 participants, but our online sample here was only half of that and thus they need replication in larger samples.

text.text: As a next step, therefore, larger and more diverse samples are needed to further examine the relational processes of our task.
Secondly, as we've discussed previously, our quantitative analyses were datadriven approaches.
While these methods are useful for uncovering patterns within the data, they lack the explanatory depth of other theory-driven approaches.
Given the high prevalence of relational dynamics (like mentalizing and moral inferences) in our task, more theory-driven modeling is required to shed light on their underlying mechanics.

Interestingly, simulation papers have shown promising results in reproducing some interesting patterns that may explain some of patterns, including idealization/devaluation of others (e.g., Story et al., 2024) or mentalizing patterns (e.g., Zavlis et al., 2026).

text.text: Our aim for future research is to apply these modeling approaches to our task and examine the relational processes our task elicits more comprehensively in order to shed light on relational dynamics from both neuro-typical and neuro-diverse populations.
Finally, we acknowledge that letting participants know they are interacting with artificial agents, may limit our ecological validity with regards to understanding real relational interactions.

Moreover, this applies to the idea of what 'realistic' means (i.e., if a participant affirms the task feels ecologically valid, it may be unclear whether they mean it feels 'realistic to real life' or 'realistic online', and they may not be aware of the difference either).

Although they put themselves in the shoes of a real-life situation, the difference between interacting with humans and role-playing without the unique stakes involved in real help-seeking may make a substantial difference.
Nevertheless, as a next step, we plan to extend our task to include real, dyadic interactions further improving its validity.
To conclude, we have developed and validated the Helping Task using a mixed qualitative and quantitative approach.
Our results showed how participants in a vulnerable position as help-seekers described meaningful relational experiences with their helpers (despite knowing they are artificial agents).

Repeated ratings of trust and satisfaction, as well as engagement throughout repeated interactions with helpers helped captured how they evaluated their helper and their own choices separately, and their willingness to continue investing.
Future work with the Helping task should include larger samples with theorydriven modelling, and real dyadic interactions to extend these preliminary findings.
